claims.text: Near-equiatomic mixtures of five or more metals can form single-phase solid-solution HEA nanoparticles.
Structural and chemical stability across 473–1923 K is governed by a balance between thermodynamic driving forces and kinetic barriers to surface and bulk diffusion.
Mixing enthalpy contributes to the formation and stability of single-phase HEAs.
Atomic-size mismatch creates strain that contributes to HEA nanoparticle stability or instability.
Kinetic constraints that sufficiently retard elemental segregation preserve the initial solid solution.
If diffusion overcomes the relevant kinetic barriers, phase separation or chemical ordering occurs.
At moderate operating temperatures, configurational entropy stabilizes a homogeneous HEA phase.
Increasing temperature enhances atomic mobility and can initiate elemental diffusion.
Strain and local bonding can create energy barriers high enough to keep diffusion slow and preserve the original structure.
Excessively negative mixing enthalpy can promote chemical ordering or phase separation when diffusion is sufficiently rapid.
Nanoparticles having moderate negative mixing enthalpy and controlled atomic-size mismatch will remain single-phase and chemically homogeneous throughout 473–1923 K.
Nanoparticles having excessive atomic-size mismatch or strongly negative mixing enthalpy will segregate and form secondary phases at high temperature.
Reactive atmospheres can independently alter nanoparticle structural stability.
Reactive gases or catalytic adsorbates can modify diffusion kinetics and surface energies.
The initial homogeneous solid solution will be characterized by X-ray diffraction and electron microscopy before thermal treatment.
A series of equimolar HEA nanoparticles with varied constituent elements will be exposed to the same 473–1923 K inert-atmosphere temperature ramp.
In situ X-ray diffraction, high-resolution TEM, and EDS mapping can be used to detect phase transitions, phase boundaries, ordering, and elemental segregation.
Segregation or ordering in nanoparticles designated as having moderate mismatch and mixing enthalpy would falsify the predicted stability.
